title: Hydrangea bush still has big green deciduous leaves, end of January | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "socalnolympia", "author_name": "socalnolympia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/socalnolympia", "date": "2026-02-01", "text": "I saw this plant, which I assume is oakleaf hydrangea, in a community garden in Olympia, WA. What struck me is the plant still has green leaves even though it is January 31, big green leaves that look like oak leaves, and look very much like the type of leaf you would expect to see on a deciduous plant. The leaves are mostly green, though parts of the leaves and a few of the leaves have turned a bronze-red color, as if it were mid-October and the leaves were just beginning to turn color and getting ready to drop off. The bush is pretty tall, almost six feet. This is in climate zone 8a. I've never seen a plant like this.     Here's some quick information I pulled up from the internet: \"Oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia) often retains its leaves, which turn a deep bronze, burgundy, or purple color, well into or throughout the winter, especially in milder climates (zones 7-9). While technically deciduous, they are known for this persistent, colorful foliage that provides significant winter interest.\" So a plant with deciduous-type big leaves is still holding its leaves late into the middle of winter. It's very rare to see a plant with leaves that look like this at this time of year, I would say.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/52426480097eb459_1385-w500-h614-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/4cf25bb3097eb45a_1389-w500-h386-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "socalnolympia", "author_name": "socalnolympia", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/socalnolympia", "date": "2026-02-01", "text": "I just found this thread: Old oakleaf hydrangea leaves not falling Apparently someone else in Santa Rosa, California, noticed that the old leaves from last year did not fall off, even as the plant was beginning to bud out new leaves. The plant is in a protected corner up against the house, off to the side of their entryway. The leaves towards the top and tips that are more exposed look mostly all bronzed over but half the leaves look more than half green, with some of the old big leaves looking mostly green and alive. (All the leaves look very slightly damaged, about half of them look like they will still survive except the tip half part of the leaf will die. Mostly looks like a live green plant that is just a little drooping and whose leaves got damaged by the cold) She said it doesn't get much colder than the upper 20s, and the location is between zone 9b and 8.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "luis-pr", "author_name": "luis_pr", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/luis-pr", "date": "2026-02-01", "text": "It can be normal with Oakleaf Hydrangeas. My Snow Queen in Texas gets unusually warm and dry winters on some La Ni\u00f1a  years like this year (winter 2025-2026) and does the same thing. Some leaves turn 'on' their fall foliage as scheduled in the fall but many leaves remain shades of green too. Then a late freeze to the single digits arrives thanks to a polar vortex, we crash from the 60s/70s to the single digits overnight and the hydrangea finally goes to sleep in mid-late January or in February. Another Oakleaf, Pee Wee, located nearby but which gets less sun exposure, turns less of a fall leaf show but usually, many of its leaves stay attached and dark green. Toy Soldier and Ruby Slippers, in other locations, tended to drop the leaves after the fall foliage show was over instead. I do worry about the flower buds getting zapped as temperatures crash here from the 70s to single digits overnight but so far, they all bloom reliably in my zone 8. Snow Queen, et al will drop the old, still attached, leaves when it is time to open the leaf buds in mid March or so; that is when the Oakleafs usually break dormancy here. Big Leaf Hydrangeas can also remain with dark green leaves or basically, actively growing in the south until December and early-mid January here and in Florida so do not panic.", "images": []}}

title: Heat vent is behind bathroom vanity - need solution to vent heat | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "marnolan51", "author_name": "marnolan51", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/marnolan51", "date": "2026-02-02", "text": "In the condo we just purchased, the previous owner installed a new vanity in front of a heat vent. There is a space filler between the cabinet and the wall so the heat is trapped by the vanity. We now have a very warm vanity interior. Should we install new doors on the front or vents on the side? Purchase a new vanity with venting? Install a vent at the top? Looking for creative ideas.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "mojavemaria", "author_name": "mojavemaria", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/mojavemaria", "date": "2026-02-02", "text": "A toekick vent with screen might work, it lets the air out under the cabinet.", "images": []}, "Comment 2": {"author_id": "marnolan51", "author_name": "marnolan51", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/marnolan51", "date": "2026-02-02", "text": "Thanks for this. How hot does the radiator get? Heat from our toaster hasn't bothered our cabinets but there is no direct contact.  Hopefully there is a gap between your radiator and cabinet back.", "images": []}, "Comment 4": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2026-02-02", "text": "The placement on which wall makes a difference, behind or beside the vanity. \"Filler\" usually means beside (because behind you'd have counter depth issues), and the width of filler matters. Also whether it is baseboard radiator heat or an in-wall unit. The problem here with radiated heat is you need adequate clearance for airflow. The toekick method is good for forced air, not for a radiator far away from the front of vanity. A picture would really help.", "images": []}, "Comment 5": {"author_id": "arpit-pfvwin-pf~1641406003", "author_name": "Arpit", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/not-specified/arpit-pfvwin-pf~1641406003", "date": "2026-02-05", "text": "You really don\u2019t want to trap a heat vent inside a vanity \u2014 it overheats the cabinet and also blocks airflow to the room. title: Is the Wolf CI36560T/S 36" Induction Cooktop Worth the Price? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "diychris24", "author_name": "Chris I", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/diychris24", "date": "2026-02-02", "text": "I am remodeling my kitchen, and I always planned to get a 36\" Wolf Induction cooktop (CI36560T/S). My sister has a generic Samsung unit, and that's where I had first used one. One of my family members recently got a Bosch 800, and I got to try it while I was staying with them during Christmas. It's really nice, and I definitely enjoyed the experience. I know some people complain about the touch controls, but I didn't have any issues. What surprised me is that I finally got to try the Wolf. I expected that I would be blown away, but I feel completely underwhelmed, especially at the price point. It doesn't feel like it's worth $4,300 to me, and as of yesterday, it's now $220 more. If I didn't know any better, I would think it's somewhere in the $3k range. I do like the touchscreen better than the Bosch, but other than that, I really didn't notice much of a performance difference. I cook primarily plant-based meals (no meat), so perhaps that has something to do with it. I thought about looking into Thermador, but they have models that are even more expensive. My question is whether I'm missing something that I wouldn't have noticed in the short time I got to use it, or if the cost has more to do with it being a premium brand.", "images": []}

title: Water-based primer: Kilz vs Zinnser vs B.M.? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "coastal-vibe", "author_name": "coastal_vibe", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/coastal-vibe", "date": "2026-02-04", "text": "Which water-based primer would you recommend for new drywall in a bathroom renovation? I need only one gallon of primer, so not concerned about cost difference Kilz Kitchen & Bath interior primer Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3 B.M. Fresh Start B.M. Multipurpose primer Paint will be selected from B.M. Aura Bath & Spa or SW Duration in satin finish", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jennifer-hogan285", "author_name": "Jennifer Hogan", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jennifer-hogan285", "date": "2026-02-10", "text": "There are going to be 40 different answers if you ask 40 different people. Paint Talk is a good forum where you can read the advice professional painters are giving each other.    They don't all agree.   Some don't prime new drywall at all, most do.   Most seem to shy away from the PVA primers and go for an all purpose primer.   Quite a few swear by Gardz.   Some  use Gardz and then paint a white primer over it since it is transparent and makes seeing flaws a bit difficult. When doing my own home I have not started with level 5 walls, so I can get away with a few things that you can't get away with if your are working with level 5 walls.   I still always wipe down my walls with a damp cloth to get rid of any dust before painting.    I don't sand between coats, but I would if I had level 5 walls. I always use one coat of primer and 2 coats of paint. I use Zinsser 123 for the walls that were not wallpapered.   I am using Gardz on the walls that were previously wall papered.   I am using BM Regal Select for my walls and Advance for my doors and trim.   I am not thrilled with Advance, and am looking at some alternatives. I have noticed some micro bubbles in Advance - most of which pop on their own within seconds of applying the paint, but I have to check the surface and use a insulin needle to pop those that have not popped so I don't see them in the finished work.  PITA On my exterior garage door and windows I used SW Duration. The one thing you will never see when I have completed a room is sloppy paint - no ceiling paint on the walls, a hairline of wall paint on the ceiling, lines between trim and walls are clean and straight. I think this is what I find most annoying when people hire pros to do their painting.  I know people who spent a fortune on the highest end paints and the finished work isn't perfectly clean.  Little drips, patches that weren't sanded well enough to appear smooth or were sanded and not textured to match the wall, outlets that have paint on them and my biggest pet peeve is ceiling paint that has gotten on the wall.   Why is it so hard to make sure the line goes on the ceiling where the eye doesn't see it? I get complements on my paint jobs from the trades people I know all the time. Each person has to know what is important to them and just how fussy they need to be to be happy with the end result. If you are hiring someone to paint I would demand that they do a primer and 2 coats of paint.  I would not specify which primer, but explain that you don't want to see any flashing where the drywall has been taped.     I also find that many painters use less product than they should.   Estimate the number of gallons needed and see how much they use.   If they spread the paint too thin it doesn't hold up as well or cover as well.   This is the main reason painters need to do a third coat of anything - if they used the appropriate amount of paint and primer 1 coat of primer and 2 coats of paint will cover.", "images": []}}

Most of these side effects were not disclosed related to using Latisse. Bimatoprost belongs to a class of medications called prostaglandin analogs (PGAs).  The side effects of PGAs are significantly risky + they extend far beyond the minor side effects acknowledged in marketing materials. From \"panda eyes\" (darkening of upper and lower eyelids), itchy, red, dry eyes to permanent iris color changes to significant orbital fat atrophy.  This condition, often termed prostaglandin-associated periorbitopathy (PAP), results in a sunken, hollowed, or aged appearance around the eyes. There is also potential thinning of eyelid skin + periocular muscle atrophy and weakness = upper eyelid ptosis (drooping). I know someone who had to have surgery to address the atrophy related to her right eye muscles. MANY products sold on Amazon (+ at other retailers) as lash/eyebrow growth serums also contain PGAs.  My sister was using one that is pretty popular (I can't remember the name).  I read the ingredients - and told her to stop using it - unless she wanted permanent changes (many of which not only age a person's appearance, but can have life altering effects). While using these type products on your eyebrow area could prevent some of the side effects - there is still PAP and periorbital muscle atrophy/weakness that has occurred + skin discoloration. Sorry for the long comment.  This is just a subject that is very upsetting to me.  I believe that I have dry eyes as a permanent side effect + I had to do a lot of eye muscle exercises in order to strengthen my right eye muscles (I still do them now - but on both eyes just to keep the muscles strong in order to prevent drooping eyelids).", "images": []}}

title: Newbie growing Dahlias in earnest this year | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "jjkoc", "author_name": "jjkOC zone 10a/22, SoCal", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jjkoc", "date": "2026-02-06", "text": "Hi all, I have contributed previously to the rose forum but this is my first time posting in the Dahlia forum. I am excited to start my Dahlia journey, despite my limited space. I have two raised beds set up in my backyard that are south facing.  I\u2019ll be filling them with premium Fox Farm Ocean Forest soil.  I anticipate my first tubers to arrive in mid-March. I\u2019m in zone 10a. My question/concern is that I\u2019ve been reading so many recommendations to quarantine new tubers in 5 gal pots for 2 years before planting into beds to mitigate the risk of spreading Dahlia gall in the soil to other susceptible plants. I bought the raised beds to reduce the clutter of pots, but I\u2019m now confused, because it seems like I will have to grow the tubers in pots anyway for 2 years! I have ordered tubers from domestic farms that seem reputable based on current reviews. All of the vendors are either those who hybridize, grow and sell, or smaller local farms that grow and sell. I selected only those who have positive reviews from multiple sources, and do not have any mentions of gall for at least a 5-year lookback. I\u2019m not sure if I am just newbie-freaking out about a reality that is low likelihood, or a natural occurrence that can be easily corrected. My thought is that if I have to grow tubers for 2 years in pots and one or more of them are infected, isn\u2019t there still a risk of all the plants becoming infected by being in the same yard? I undertand that I should bleach my shears per plant, but wouldn\u2019t any soil or water spilled from any pot containing an infected plant contaminate the surrounding area? In which case, I would then have to place water-catch dishes under each pot? And if I were to dig up each plant at the end of the season and find an infected plant, then I would have to toss the pot with soil, let alone the washed tuber? other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "jacqueline9ca", "author_name": "jacqueline9CA", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/jacqueline9ca", "date": "2026-02-07", "text": "The main thing I have learned after inheriting a garden with lots of roses in it already which were planted in the prior 80 ish years, and then gardening for 35 years, is that there is NO one way to prune roses. It depends entirely on WHAT KIND of rose it is, and your climate. I always cringe in the very early Spring here (Northern  Calif, zone 9/10, Mediterranean climate) when the local Rose society, and some nurseries, put on free classes on \"how to prune roses\". These usually are really  classes on \"How to prune modern hybrid tea roses\". They do a fine job on that, but that ignores the several other classes of roses which actually prefer our type of climate over any other, and thrive here with much less fussing. The old tea roses and old hybrid china roses which thrive in my garden do NOT want to be pruned hard like modern hybrid teas. Over the years when one of those inadvertantly DID get hard pruned, they sulked for actual years before gradually recovering, if they did indeed recover.  The ones in my garden like to be mainly left alone, other than taking out dead wood (sometimes this is not even a good idea, if a large bush has built up dead wood as a sort of scafolding support under the rest of the bush), shaping a bit, and keeping them OFF of the driveway and paths (some of the old teas and chinas have \"I am going to conquer the world\"complexes). The old Vintage Roses catalog has wonderful drawings of each type of old rose, its growth habit, and how to prune it if you want to. I do have a very few HTs, all surviors from previous generations of my DH's family. Interestingly, most of the bush types of those have died. The ones still alive are all climbers. I think that most of those started out as bushes, and then reverted to climbing because of local conditions. Of course, then do need pruning, tying up, etc. We have lots of other types of old roses, and none of them react well by being pruned according to the \"rules\" for pruning HTs bushes. title: How do location & surroundings affect a dream house? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lucajack27", "author_name": "Lucajack jack", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lucajack27", "date": "2026-02-10", "text": "Location and environment play a crucial role in shaping both the design and value of a dream house. The surrounding climate, terrain, and natural features directly influence architectural choices, materials, and energy efficiency. For example, coastal homes may require corrosion-resistant materials and elevated foundations, while mountain houses need insulation and sturdy roofing to withstand snow. Proximity to amenities like schools, workplaces, shops, and recreational areas also affects design priorities, such as the inclusion of home offices, garages, or outdoor living spaces. A serene, scenic environment can increase the property\u2019s market value, while a noisy or congested area may require soundproofing and privacy-focused design. Additionally, local zoning laws, building codes, and environmental regulations guide the layout, height, and footprint of the home. Smart consideration of location and environment ensures that a dream house is not only beautiful but also functional, sustainable, and valuable over time.", "images": []}

title: Doors That Elevate Your Home’s Style | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "seven-pfvwus-pf~1767221271", "author_name": "Seven", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/commercial-construction/seven-pfvwus-pf~1767221271", "date": "2026-02-11", "text": "I\u2019ve spent a lot of time thinking about how doors tie a home\u2019s design together, and it\u2019s always the small, intentional choices that make the biggest difference. So I wanted to share a few thoughts on pairingdoor styles with different home aesthetics\u2014something that\u2019s easy to overlook but totally transforms the feel of every room, especially when you\u2019re building a home from the ground up. For cottage or Lowcountry styles, keep it warm and understated. Flat panel doors with subtle, thin raised molding hit the sweet spot\u2014too much ornate carving can feel clunky, while plain slabs lack the rustic charm this aesthetic is all about. Stick to natural wood tones: honeyed oak, soft pine, or light maple, and opt for simple brass or black iron hardware with a slightly worn finish. If you have front entry sidelights, go for glass with thin wooden muntins; it adds light without breaking the cozy, organic vibe. For modern minimalist or open-concept builds, clean lines are non-negotiable. Frameless flat slab doors are perfect here\u2014they blend into the walls and keep the space feeling uncluttered. Stick to a single finish across these doors: matte white paint, light white oak with a clear matte seal, or even dark walnut for a bold contrast against light walls. Invisible hinges and flush, pull-less hardware take the sleekness a step further, and matching the door tone to your floor trim creates a seamless flow through the open space. For classic traditional homes, raised panel doors are the foundation, but pay attention to scale. If you have 10ft ceilings (a common ask in new builds!), go for taller 8ft or 9ft doors with double raised panels\u2014they draw the eye up and make rooms feel grander. Cherry wood or rich red oak with a warm stain pairs beautifully with crown molding, hardwood floors, and marble accents, and polished brass or oil-rubbed bronze hardware ties the classic look together. Just avoid overcrowding the panels; simple, balanced detailing is key. A quick little tip that makes a huge impact: keep your door palette cohesive, not identical. It\u2019s fine to use a moisture-resistant wood composite for bathrooms/laundry rooms (practicality first!) as long as it\u2019s stained or painted to match your solid wood interior doors, and stick to the same hardware finish throughout the house. It keeps the design intentional without sacrificing function. Doors are so much more than just a functional part of a home\u2014they\u2019re a quiet design statement that shapes how every room feels. Hope these little insights help as you build your dream space!", "images": []}

title: Ways to Vent a Garage Ceiling....Tastefully? | Houzz Forum

The garage is 30' X 40' with 12' walls and a 4/12 roof pitch.  My open-cell spray-foam contractor recommended insulating the under side of the roof rather than insulating the top of the ceiling.  The walls have 4\" of foam and the underside of the roof has 6\".  So, I ditched my plans to vent the attic space to the outside...no soffet vents, no gable vents, no ridge vents.  I'm putting up PVC corrugated panels for the ceiling and now have a decent minds-eye for how that will look...and can envision different openings in the ceiling to vent attic space air down into the room space.  I'm not crazy about big, square, black holes and I really have no idea how many square feet of opening area I should have to adequately vent the attic.  I do have HVAC and the air handler is already in the attic and ready to be set up by my HVAC guy.  BUT, I don't plan to run that unit enough for it to serve as the attic venting solution.  I love single-room dehumidifiers and will be using one on a timer in the garage to keep the humidity down.  It's more economical I think than running the HVAC unit just for humidity control. For simplicity and economic reasons, I would prefer venting to be passive, so I expect to need more square feet of vent openings than if I had a forced-air vent.  I could go with solar-powered vent fans if battery maintenance doesn't become an issue (time and $$). Cut several square, round, or oval holes in the PVC ceiling on each end of the 40 ft ceiling length and depend on passive air exchange. B.  Cut similar holes and fit with white metal HVAC grates to help the look.  Cut smaller holes on each end and fit with solar fans (several blowing up and several blowing down) to force-circulate air. C. Put the attic HVAC unit on a timer and run the fan 5-10 minutes several times a day.  HVAC intake would be in the attic and the vents would be through-ceiling. I used to get 20-50 blooms on a single cane of Bishop's Castle, but I haven't had that in the last few years no matter what pruning technique I use. I've tried three options, but have not been satisfied with the results of any. 1. Thin out the twiggy growth at the top but leave them. The result is small flowers on small twiggy growth at the tops of the canes, and a very short bloom season. I've also tried cutting off most of the twiggy stuff until it is down to pencil thickness and leaving the broomstick trunk. I'm left with a broomstick with a tuft on top. 2. title: Choosing a 30" Gas Range | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "rslifkin-pfvwus-pf~131439372", "author_name": "rslifkin", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/rslifkin-pfvwus-pf~131439372", "date": "2026-02-12", "text": "I'm in the process of planning some minor kitchen upgrades.  We're not changing countertops or cabinets (beyond removing the cabinet above the current over the range microwave to replace it with a proper hood).  So we're limited to a 30\" range.  There's currently gas, but no 240V power to the range location, so I'd prefer to stay with an all-gas range for ease of install. Currently we have an older Kenmore range, but it has a couple of weak points.  It only has 1 higher powered burner (17k BTU).  I'd really like at least a second higher power burner (next most powerful on the current range is 9500 BTU).  And something more than the current 17k on the highest powered burner would be good, as I've found the current burner a little weak at times with a wok or for searing.  The current burners are also pretty terrible for heat distribution, as they flare out to the sides badly at high power settings (the power burner will have the hottest point right at the edges of a 12\" skillet for example).  We've been happy enough with the current oven (neither of us is a big baker), so any oven that's at least decent will be fine, and there's no real need for a double oven range. The easy answer for a good upgrade in my mind would be something like a Bluestar RNB or Capital Culinarian.  But this isn't going to be a forever house and doesn't necessarily have the perfect kitchen design currently either, so I don't think it really makes sense to spend $5000+ on a range. Currently, the front runner in my mind is the 30\" Cafe 6 burner single oven (CGS700P2MS1, $2700).  The ability to swap the center grate for a griddle is a nice to have, it has a 21k BTU tri ring for the most powerful burner, and also has a 15k and a 12k in addition to the lower powered burners.  And the layout seems good for a 30\" setup, as the 2 center burners (as opposed to one oval) would allow use of 3x 12\" pans at the same time (front corners and back center) without pushing the pans off-center on the burners.  My biggest concern is about heat flare out to the sides with the big burner for use with a wok, etc. I have found a couple of other possible options that look reasonable.  One is the Frigidaire PCFG3080AF ($2400).  It's also 6 burners, but lower powered and none of them are multi-ring or anything.  The most powerful are 18k, and the \"standard\" size burners are only 7500 BTU instead of 9500, so I worry about having enough power and heat distribution problems on the big burners, although the flame holes do appear a little better placed to let flames go upward instead of just outward compared to the typical mushroom cap burners I have now (and the GE has for 5 of the 6). Another possible option is the Electrolux ECFG3068AS ($3200).  It's more expensive than the other options and also has the somewhat less useful oval center burner (fine for a griddle but nothing else).  The front burners are also only 18k on this range, but both rears are 12k.  And they appear to all be multi-ring, plus the outer rings have the flame holes on the top of the cap angled up and outward, so at first glance it looks like they'd have a bit less outward flare and might distribute heat better. What does everyone here think might be the best of those options?  And what other options are out there that I might have missed that have decent burners?", "images": []}

title: Initial late winter (meteorological) yard tree (conifers) report. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bill-mn_z3b", "author_name": "BillMN-z4a", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bill-mn_z3b", "date": "2026-02-12", "text": "With other threads veering off the subject of condition of plants, both protected and unprotected from varmints and winter in general, I finally got out today to check over the yard today. I first wanted to check the smaller trees that were covered with snow, both by snowfall and me shoveling, to make sure I wasn't going to crush any of them as the snow melted. What generally happens on huge piles of snow, it can slowly melt just from its own weight, turning it into a solid mass of frozen snow, like ice and the whole thing can slide in a sideways direction, doing damage to the plant as the mass descends downward during the spring thaw. With smaller plants and small snow piles, it isn't as concerning and you generally, you will get an ice 'shell' with loose snow inside, but with small tender plants, it's worth checking during winter, JIC. My first to be inspected were, of course, the two newest acquisitions just planted last summer. 1) Abies Nordmanniana: The top was a little 'off center' when the leader began appearing out the top of the snow, to me that's a red flag. So, I had a 2 ft. length of base board to gently chop and shovel the outer ice shell and move some of the snow away to take any pressure off the plant. Turns out, the top was a little off kilter, and top branches were aligned somewhat downward, but I've seen worse, and as the snow continues to melt, I think it will be just fine. I doubt we'll get any more damaging (-30+), severe temperatures from now on so the plant can be exposed now (with sun protection).  2) Picea Omorika: This one was most concerning because of its soft, flexible nature, although trees like this grow in winter conditions with high snow fall amounts. The main leader was showing about an inch out of the snow and looked centered. The snow pile only had a 'shell' of ice on the surface, and the snow underneath had a sugar like texture. So carefully, not to hit the branches or needles, I removed enough snow, halfway down, that the above freezing temperatures will clear/melt the top half for me, in the next couple of days, even though the ground will still have some snow cover for the roots.  3) Thuja plicata 'Virescens': This is a second-year plant and was coming out of the snow practically all by itself. but I helped it a little bit bc it was tipping a little to one side. nbd. Abies. I found the rabbits were still working on the left side on a couple of previously chewed on branches but had left the rest, even the exposed branch on the right, unscathed! The jack pine had just a smidgen of damage most likely from an immature bunny that didn't know he wouldn't like pine. So, nbd.  Same for the young red pine: I've never protect the pine before and never had rabbit damage.  I protected the P. Cembra just because of the $$ but the only thing I could see there was the little note left on the CW that said 'Thanks for Nothing'. \ud83e\udd23  Another tree I never had rabbit damage on is the Abies balsamea: The lower branches don't get enough sun to grow well but it never appears to be 'nipped' at all when I check it and never have put CW around it (rabbit tracks going right by it).  Another plant I never protect is the Taunton Yew. title: Omnibus Mid-Atlantic/DC/Philly/NY winter 2026 damage and recovery | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "upperbaygardener", "author_name": "UpperBayGardener (zone 7)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/upperbaygardener", "date": "2026-02-14", "text": "I think it makes the most sense for these to be shared among participants in a given region. That's why I didn't glom onto Bill's conifer report.  But anyone else in the upper midwest should do so. Took my first long 30 minute walk around today, because it's the first day in 20 days that isn't below normal! Speaking in generalities, here are themes I'm seeing: 1) the incredible power of snow cover.  My Camellia 'Yume' is considered a not-especially hardiness selected variety, some catalogs used to rate it as 8a or 7b...but it was near my driveway so while clearing snow with bucket and blade, decided to cover it as much as possible.  Thank goodness I did think to do this while the snow was still a little loose and not completely icy yet. (If nothing else, it was to mechanically protect it from the snow I was going to have to later pile in that area) There's enough melting to expose a bit of it, and it looks totally undamaged. Contrast with a 'rated 6b' tea plant in the worst possible environment: denied some early 'wrapping' snow cover because of overhanging conifer branches, and way too tall to be completely snow covered, on a south slope w/o protection from winter morning sun that I'm always harping on as important*, but still exposed to reflected snow.  It looks absolutely awful.  Some of the worst camellia damage I've seen since I started growing camellias at my parent's house in 1994. Before the snow got icy I rushed to scoop it onto some rare BLEs like the variegated Lithocarpus edulis - and wow, I'm glad I did.  I have no doubt that without it, that would have been severely injured.  Other than a branchlet I broke because the snow was starting to be icy, it looks just fine.  Seeing how powerful even this icy snow was at protecting things, makes me a little less worried about, for example, my expanding outdoor Hedychium collection.  But I'll still be worried until I see shoots! 2) the wisdom of the USDA zone system.  Although I already sort of knew this, it's illustrating to compare last winter's brief dip to 2F, to this winter's prolonged and repeated excursions to 8F or so.   Of course in the 1950s or whenever Wyman, Harvard & the USDA were developing the zone map system, they didn't have the ability to number crunch that we would now w/computers.   A station's annual lowest recorded temp was easier to get.  But I'm going to compare the 'number crunching' based system the Atlas of Woody Plants of China uses.  I should dignify it by posting the actual definition, but it's something like the number of degree days below 3C.  Very difficult to calculate until recently, but, especially in a climate w/China's stable winter weather is perhaps a more human relatable measure of 'how chilly a place is'.   But looking at plants in that volume and their ratings versus what I know their USDA zones to be, I know it's just not a good system for subtropical and temperate woody plant hardiness. (could make more sense for truly tropical plants)  It is abundantly clear now that at least w/respect to cold tolerance, a couple nights of 0F really is much worse than a winter of 20 nights of 10F  - all other things being equal, of course, which they never are(!) - for most, but not all, plants on that particular edge of hardiness.  So for example, my Trachycarpus was definitely looking more injured after last winter, although still, for it, not nearly as badly as some prior cold winters.  (It's been fully defoliated twice since I planted it in spring 2015) 3) the power of provenance and selection.  For example, one thing I'm 'tremendously chuffed' about (love that silly UK expression) is that my Taiwania looks totally undamaged.  ALL of my California redwoods, even the largest, are at least showing a bit of damage, like snow line reflected light burning.  Not this Taiwania which I believe was selected in the SE US for hardiness.  Because I have a Taiwania from Sheffield seed - Chinese seed origin - where the one I planted out last winter died, dead as a doornail.  Even though it was almost 1/4\" caliper and about 2' tall...past the stage of looking like a tiny seedling.  Based on how well the selected one has done, I don't believe more years would have helped the seedling.  I strongly suspect it just wasn't from a stain selected for hardiness, since the Chinese don't have to do that in their own environment.  (maybe some crazy guy wants to grow Taiwanias in, say, Beijing, but if so, they are keeping their hardy seed for themselves) So, in fairness to Sheffield, I would say they are correct in offering that strain as 8 to 10 hardy https://sheffields.com/seeds-for-sale/Taiwania/cryptomerioides///////697830/Chinese-Coffin-Tree,-Coffin-Tree,-Taiwania/Chinese-Coffin-Tree,-Coffin-Tree,-Taiwania But it's obvious the one I got at Appeldoorn in Feb 2023 (best one shot nursery visit ever!) is easily at least 7b hardy.  Time will tell how it will respond when I inevitably go below 5F, which I'm sure will happen again.   Leading me to...drumroll please... 4) The mixed blessing of the most recent USDA zone map revision. It moved coastal Cecil county from having patches of 7b, to being almost entirely in 7b, and this winter seemingly proved the correctness of that.  But you only had to go 15-20 miles to the north to find newly minted 7a areas, that I think might have been better if they'd stayed in 6b.  Because they were dropping to around -5F if not lower,  this winter, and have done so in recent winters as well.  A lot of palm and subtropical plant collectors in central Florida are feeling 'burned' by the latest revision, to say the least!  [Since people willfully 'misuse' or 'misinterpret' the USDA system, there's almost a case for revising how it works, period, but I won't go into that for now] 5) All I've learned about smart planting since the Polar Vortex winters of 2013-2015.  But I'll follow up with this as I post more details observations in the month ahead.  Big picture here is, dodged a bullet!  Because of 1) correct plant siting 2) emergency measures (covering stuff w/snow) and 3) a bit of luck! * - 6) rereading this after posting, I'm struck that the need to protect tenderish BLEs from winter morning sun was strikingly evidenced by this winter, too.", "images": []}

We finished planting at the end of the year, but, being a gardener, I'm projected toward the future, and already planning what's going to go in the ground this coming fall. Meanwhile, spring is on the way, a little too early for my taste.  The early crocuses are in bloom, as are the sarcococcas, primroses, snowdrops, hellebores, shrub honeysuckle, and others. A couple of weeks more, though, and spring will truly and legitimately be under way. title: The Wet Area Guide: The Importance of Proper Shower Screen Sealing and | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "alvi-a", "author_name": "alvi A", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/alvi-a", "date": "2026-02-18", "text": "Wet areas demand careful planning and precise installation to protect bathrooms from long-term moisture damage. Shower screens are a central component of this protection, yet their performance depends heavily on correct sealing and waterproofing. Without proper techniques, water can escape the shower zone, leading to leaks, mold growth, and structural deterioration. Homeowners installing glass panel shower screens for baths in Australia, or upgrading existing shower screens for baths, benefit most when sealing and waterproofing are treated as essential design and safety measures rather than asfinishing details. Understanding wet areas and water exposure Bathrooms are classified as wet areas because they are constantly exposed to water, steam, and humidity. Shower zones are especially vulnerable due to direct splashing and water pressure. Even small gaps around shower screens allow water to migrate beneath tiles or behind walls. Over time, this hidden moisture weakens adhesives, damages substrates, and compromises flooring. Proper sealing ensures that water remains contained within the shower area, preserving the integrity of surrounding surfaces. Why sealing matters for shower screens Shower screen sealing creates a watertight barrier between glass panels, walls, and floors. High-quality seals prevent water from escaping through joints and edges during daily use. Silicone sealants and precision-fitted gaskets are commonly used to seal gaps while allowing slight movement due to temperature changes. For shower screens in baths, where water frequently strikes the lower edge of the glass, sealing is especially critical to prevent leaks along the tub rim and at the floor junctions. Waterproofing techniques behind the scenes Waterproofing works beneath visible surfaces to protect the bathroom structure. Before shower screens are installed, waterproof membranes should be applied to walls and floors in accordance with building standards. These membranes act as a secondary defense if surface seals fail. Proper slope toward drains, secure membrane overlaps, and reinforced corners all contribute to effective water management. When combined with well-installed glass panel shower screens for baths in Australia, these techniques significantly reduce the risk of water damage. Common sealing mistakes to avoid Poor preparation is a leading cause of seal failure. Applying sealant to dusty or damp surfaces prevents proper adhesion. Inconsistent bead thickness and missed corners also create weak points where water can escape. Using low-grade sealants that are not designed for wet areas increases the likelihood of cracking and discoloration. Professional installation or careful adherence to manufacturer guidelines helps avoid these issues and ensures long-lasting performance. Maintenance and inspection for long-term protection Even the best sealing systems require periodic inspection. Sealants can degrade over time due to constant moisture and cleaning products. Homeowners should regularly check for gaps, peeling, or mold along the edges of the shower screen. Prompt resealing extends the lifespan of shower screens for baths and prevents minor issues from escalating into costly repairs. Gentle cleaning methods also help preserve seal integrity. Choosing quality materials and installation High-quality materials play a vital role in waterproof performance. Toughened glass, precision hardware, and moisture-resistant sealants contribute to a reliable system. Reputable suppliers offering glass panel shower screens for baths in Australia typically design products that support effective sealing and long-term durability. Selecting compatible components and ensuring accurate installation improves both safety and functionality. Protecting your bathroom investment Proper shower screen sealing and waterproofing are foundational to a durable, hygienic bathroom. These techniques protect structural elements, enhance usability, and support long-term value. Whether installing new shower screens for baths or maintaining existing systems, prioritizing correct sealing practices ensures that wet areas remain secure, efficient, and visually appealing for years to come.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/13a2b6db09956df1_0689-w500-h500-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

title: Is anyone still here? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "dirty-gardener", "author_name": "dirtygardener", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dirty-gardener", "date": "2026-02-19", "text": "Hi all! I'm mostly on Reddit now, where I started a Gainesville Gardening group (r/gainesvillegardening) and a Florida Gardening group (r/floridagardening), but I had to turn the Florida group over to someone else after just being overwhelmed from health problems last year. Last year was a rough year. I'm getting old now (73 -- will be 74 in May). It's hard to believe it's been almost 30 years since I first posted on Gardenweb in 1996. I don't garden as much anymore, in fact, I'm trying to sell a lot of my larger plants to ease my load. I had to have two serious eye surgeries in 2026. I had cataract surgery and glaucoma surgery in both eyes, six months apart. Couldn't garden because I couldn't bend over or lift, so my yard and gardens went to hell in a handbasket. After this latest freeze, I'm still cleaning up. Didn't lose much, just some small plants I thought would be o.k., but they weren't. Luckily, they were just babies and the mama plants are fine. I still have so many of the plants I got from y'all. My fig trees are in 10 gallon pots and doing well, but I'm moving them up to 15 gallons this year. I still have three brugs, but they're do-overs because of all the neglect last year. I still have my plumeria and dragon fruit. The pink cane begonia almost died last summer due to so much rain, but I managed to save some cuttings, so it's being babied now. Still have the pink Hawaiian confederate rose someone sent me seeds for that they had smuggled into the US sewed into the hem of a dress. It never puts out seeds here, because there aren't many pollinators here in the city, but I still root cuttings every year and give them away. Still have my staghorn that has tried to die on me three times, but it's finally doing really well. The hibiscus radiatus someone sent me seeds for way back when still volunteers all over the yard in the spring. I've found a lot of bromeliads that grow well here, so I've made a bed with nothing but large broms, and I have small ones all over the place. Right now, I'm going to try to start growing veggies again, at least some easy ones. I can't eat tomatoes because of reflux, and I don't have any full sun to grow them in anyway. I bought a lot of edible weed seeds and old-timey plant seeds like salsify. I can't wait to plant those this year. Hope you are all doing well and are still around somewhere. If you want to come over to Reddit and join the Florida Gardening forum, I still post there, even though I'm mostly on the Gainesville one I run. The Gainesville forum is for anyone in Alachua county and surrounding areas. We even have some Lakeland area people there. It's a nice place. Love you all, and sorry I've been gone so long. Deborah", "images": []}

title: Ideen für den Flur | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "anna-aladjov", "author_name": "Anna K", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anna-aladjov", "date": "2026-02-19", "text": "Ihr Lieben,Wir ziehen in eine tolle neue Wohnung. Allerdings sind wir sehr ratlos, wie wir den Flur gestalten. Es soll modern und freundlich wirken und nicht so vollgestellt wirken. Wir haben zwei kleine Kinder.  Rechts hinten neben der T\u00fcre ist eine ca. 1m breite Nische. Wir w\u00fcrden uns sehr \u00fcber gute Tipps freuen. Haben leider noch nicht wirklich Ma\u00dfe, da wir noch nicht in der Wohnung sind. Danke euch ! :-)", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/2a027a060996bdff_6765-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "hu-638468403-pfvwde-pf~886413949", "author_name": "HU-638468403", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/hznb/professionals/hu-638468403-pfvwde-pf~886413949", "date": "2026-03-03", "text": "Gl\u00fcckwunsch zur neuen Wohnung! \ud83d\ude0a Gerade mit zwei kleinen Kindern w\u00fcrde ich im Flur auf eine klare, ruhige Gestaltung setzen. Helle Farben an den W\u00e4nden (z.B. warmes Wei\u00df oder ein sehr sanftes Beige) lassen den Raum sofort freundlicher wirken. Wenn der Flur nicht vollgestellt wirken soll, helfen geschlossene L\u00f6sungen \u2013 also eher ein schmaler Schrank oder eine integrierte Garderobe statt viele einzelne M\u00f6belst\u00fccke. Die 1 m breite Nische ist eigentlich ein Gl\u00fccksfall. Dort k\u00f6nnte man z.B. eine ma\u00dfgefertigte Garderobenl\u00f6sung oder eine Kombination aus Sitzbank mit Stauraum und Haken dar\u00fcber einplanen. Gerade mit Kindern ist eine Bank zum Schuheanziehen super praktisch \u2013 idealerweise mit Schubladen oder K\u00f6rben darunter. Spiegel sind ebenfalls wichtig im Flur: Sie lassen den Raum gr\u00f6\u00dfer wirken und bringen mehr Licht hinein. Wenn ihr es modern m\u00f6gt, k\u00f6nntet ihr mit einem schlichten Konsolentisch arbeiten \u2013 vielleicht aus Holz oder auch aus Betonoptik, wenn ihr es etwas puristischer m\u00f6gt \u2013 aber wirklich nur ein bewusst gew\u00e4hltes St\u00fcck, damit es nicht \u00fcberladen aussieht. Und mein wichtigster Tipp: Erst einziehen, Ma\u00dfe nehmen und ein paar Tage im Raum \u201eleben\u201c. Oft merkt man erst dann, wo wirklich Stauraum fehlt und wie der Alltag mit Kindern dort abl\u00e4uft. Viel Freude beim Planen!", "images": []}}

Thing is, I do not enjoy exercise. I have done SO many different things throughout my life, as most of us have I think. Aerobics classes, swimming, water aerobics, work out videos, that Billy Blanks thing, walking, running, dance workouts, weight training, cross fit, I mean the list goes on and on and on. I have been told by gym enthusiasts how addicting it can be when you find the right workout. I have given up on finding joy in it. I purposely make time for physical activity because it is important to my health. Thats it. I would really be happy to be a certified couch potato, but I do not want the health consequences of such. I walk 7-10 miles a day. I set myself a 15000 step a day minimum and usually meet that. I started wearing a weighted vest a few years ago while walking to increase calorie burn and I heard that it also improves bone strength. And I weight train at home a couple times a week. title: Pruning at Time of Planting | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "brandon7-gw", "author_name": "brandon7 TN_zone7", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/brandon7-gw", "date": "2026-02-22", "text": "A few years ago, some of you helped me edit a tree planting guide which became a pretty useful tool.  Today I was trying to respond to someone's inquiry about pruning fruit trees (or any tree for that matter) at time of planting.  I realized it might be worth writing a little about so I could save my response for future conversations.  Can you look over the text below and see if you see anything I left out, grammar mistakes, etc.  I know it doesn't cover HOW to prune, but I don't think I will include that (it can be covered separately).  Let me know what you would change: 1. Dead, diseased, rubbing, and heavily damaged (split, denuded, etc) limbs should be removed immediately at any time of year, including at time of planting. 2. Trees should be trained/pruned for proper form early in their life. Correcting structural issues can become much more difficult as the tree gets larger. 3. Significant pruning of healthy branches (that would result in lots of foliage loss, reduction in the number of apical buds (shoot tips), and reduction of considerable amounts of energy-storing xylem) should be avoided at time of planting. It\u2019s still very common, despite research showing disadvantages, to see recommendations by nurseries, and even some educational resources, to prune trees and shrubs at the time of planting. There are multiple reasons for this, and I will cover the most common ones. One reason is that it used to be thought that balancing the ratio of top growth (shoots/foliage) with root mass was important to the health of the tree. This has long been debunked. Properly dug/prepared trees can survive and actually become established much more quickly if top growth is left. The growth of tree roots is triggered/driven mostly by the hormone indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). IAA is produced in apical buds (shoot tips), so, if we cut back a lot of the top growth of a newly planted tree, we discourage the tree from further developing its root system by reducing production of IAA. Pruning also reduces the tree\u2019s ability to produce energy, needed for root growth, by reducing the amount of foliage which is where photosynthesis produces energy. Stored energy is also decreased because of the loss of xylem, where energy is stored. All of these factors inhibit the tree\u2019s ability to become established quickly and present increased opportunity for poor health and pest/disease issues. A second reason pruning at the time of planting may be recommended is to improve the structure of the tree. This is especially the case for fruit trees where lower scaffold branching may be desired. It is indeed important to address structural issues as early as possible. Correcting them can become more difficult as the tree gets larger. However, there\u2019s nothing magical about making the necessary changes during the planting process. This is often one of, if not THE, most stressful times during the life of the tree. Waiting until the tree becomes better established before major pruning can allow the tree to overcome this difficult time more effectively, and the necessary training/pruning can be carried out after that hurdle is overcome. A third reason for the recommendation to prune at the time of planting is because some writers may be trying to take into account that many people may plant-and-forget the tree. This is a valid concern and may fit a majority of cases, but I\u2019m not convinced it is a reason to present the option as a best practice. The ideal time to prune most ESTABLISHED trees, in our part of the world, is late winter or very early spring, after the coldest parts of winter are over but before the spring flush of growth begins. If a young tree is planted at the optimal time (mid to late fall, just after or around the time of leaf drop), it is likely to be established enough for structural pruning by that spring. A large percentage of root growth occurs, in most types of trees, during late fall and early winter after leaf drop. So, the tree can be ready for pruning relatively quickly. If the tree is planted in the spring, when many nurseries offer their trees for sale, a better time to prune would be late winter/very early spring of the following year, once the tree has developed a decent root structure and is able to vigorously cover over its wounds and begin growing correctly. In either case, the pruning will have been done in plenty of time to avoid lots of extra effort. One last thing I want to cover is how some sources, especially when talking about fruit trees, may give you a certain height to which you should head back your young tree. The suggestion is made to encourage scaffolding branch development. Different types of fruit trees tend to do better with one or more specific structure styles. Different styles will affect things like ease of maintenance, ease of harvesting, fruit production, health of the tree, etc., etc. Examples of these styles are \u201ccentral leader\u201d, \u201cmodified central leader\u201d, \u201copen center\u201d, \u201cespalier\u201d, and \u201ctall spindle\u201d. There is no one-size-fits-all approach to structure style. You should absolutely give some thought as to which style your tree should follow before any structural pruning! Also, if you plan to mow around your tree, think about how high your lowest scaffold branch should be to avoid problems.", "images": []}

title: The Tao of Pruning? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "upperbaygardener", "author_name": "UpperBayGardener (zone 7)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/upperbaygardener", "date": "2026-02-22", "text": "Or 'Zen and the Art of Not Having your Handiwork with a Chainsaw Noticed'!  I would almost combine this with Brandon's recently started thread, but 1) I'd planned it before I saw his \ud83e\udd23 and 2) it doesn't necessarily overlap - in fact, in a way, it's oddly complementary. I took advantage of the first warm day in what feels like forever yesterday to break out the chainsaw and do some winter pruning, before we return to another few days of frozen hellscape. The things I worked on 1) My largest lacebark pine.  Not sharing pics of this because it's hard to get w/o showing my neighbor's property behind it, and I value protecting their privacy as I hope they'd protect mine. 2) first time I've had to do major work on one of my larches.  These lower branches were blocking my driveway.   I'd clipped the ends of them back with loppers, but over time, that actually looks worse than this IMHO.  It's inevitable that this kind of pruning, looks like a tree has been pruned.   3) My now huge Chilopsis on the SW corner of my house. Just before the snow a month ago, I got one water sprout out of my Cedrus 'Shalimar'.  I feel like it's likely to be the last time I have to find and remove one of them on this.   (In case I forget to or don't have time to finish my hardiness reports, 'Shalimar' was of course completely fine this winter, as you can see.  But in my travels a week ago in the suburbs of Philly, I saw a smaller deodar cedar, maybe planted in the past 5 years, that was clearly burnt.  Showing that inferior, less hardy seedlings of that tree continue to be sold in areas where they shouldn't!  Thank you, greedy American wholesale plant industry.) But for the Desert Willow, the Cedar, and the Lacebark pine, I realized that my final evaluative criteria for pruning is always would it look to an average person like it's been pruned? If it doesn't,  I feel like I've been doing the right thing!  Key difference: have been doing, not \"have done\".  If I'd put off doing anything to them before now, there would be no way for corrective pruning not to be noticed. For all 3 of these plants, I've pruned them at least every other year for the past 5 to 10 years.  And so, to relate this to Brandon's post - sure you can prune something right when it's planted.  But the more important thing, in my opinion, is that consistently keep applying your vision to the plant over the years, so that it looks as good as it can. In the case of the Cedar above, in particular, I can guarantee you if I hadn't started about 11 years ago, it would have the ugly (to me) appearance of multiple trunks.  As it stands now, maybe an expert on C. d. would find the lack of lower branches slightly suspect.  And yes, I feel like the most aggressive prune I made was the lower most, left branch, but it was shading out my precious (to me LOL) 'hardiest clone of Amaryllis belladonna' which is just on the left edge of this view.  But I think, overall, a typical visitor to the garden sees this and thinks it mostly, naturally grew this way. title: Speed Queen TR5 overflowing a 2" standpipe. SOLVED! | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "lisa-wellington1", "author_name": "lisa_wellington1", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/lisa-wellington1", "date": "2026-02-23", "text": "After spending $600 on a plumber (snaking the line) , the standpipe still overflowed. I did more research and learned that for every 12\" of standpipe height, the machine will drain 1 gallon per min. slower. That's all it needed. It is called a stand pipe because that's where the water stands as it drains out.I went to my local hardware store and asked them to cut a 2\" ABS pipe to 12\", and get me a connecter and some plumbers cement. I connected the pipe with connector to my existing standpipe to test before cementing. Voila! Even on huge loads, no problem with overflow. Cost: $11.54.I called the plumber later to report this finding and asked why this solution was not offered. main_question: {"author_id": "retiredinmi", "author_name": "retiredinmi", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/retiredinmi", "date": "2026-02-25", "text": "Hi, all..considering the Blue Star Range (or more likely, Range Top) and am seeing some wildly conflicting info on Back Guard requirements. I've called Blue Star to ask directly, but not easy AT ALL to get ahold of anyone who can answer as they say Tech Support is only for Installers, so am reaching out here also. Range/Rangetop would be 30'' and installed directly against kitchen wall (ie: 0 clearance). It would appear from the Install instructions (which I've read many times, front to back) that you can use ceramic tile above (which we have) and below (which we'd need to add) for 6'' on top of a drywall/wood stud wall and be in compliance. I've seen many older threads here disagreeing with that take, and telling people to either use the 6'' min steel backguard or tear apart the wall to rebuild with steel studs and cement board (crazy!) But if we read the CURRENT install requirements, they clearly say.. \"When a unit is installed with any other back guard in a zero clearance condition, noncombustible/heat resistant materials are to be used in a vertical plane for a minimum distance of 6\u201d below the top horizontal plane of the unit and at least equal in height to the back guard being used. The non-combustible material need not extend horizontally past the initial barriers thickness. The initial barrier should consist of materials such as ceramic tile, cement backer board, stainless steel (.032\u201d Thick) or other non-combustible material\" So, am I right in thinking the specs have been updated by BlueStar at some point after all the initial discussion here about steel stud/cement board walls, etc? It would sure appear to be so. BTW, I've seen the discussion about Mechanical Codes. But there does not appear to be ANYTHING in those codes that are specific to BTU output requiring the \"minimum distances\" documented. So, that would mean NO RANGE could be installed without a backguard/steel stud walls, etc.  However, there are plenty of ranges as we all know that can, and the install docs for those ranges say absolutely nothing about not being able to install with zero clearance to rear wall without a backguard. Strangely, some of those ranges (eg: GE Cafe Gas 30'') have similar rear burner BTU output to a BlueStar RCS or RNB 30''. The GE is 26.5K across all 3 rear burners on the six-burner range and the BlueStar RCS & RNB are both 24K total across the 2 rear burners.  Yet, GE doesn't even MENTION a back guard, even though it's higher rear BTU. Incidentally, the Thermador 30'' Dual Fuel also does not mention backguard requirements even though it's open burner (star burners) as well. I've read the pyrolysis discussions, but it would appear from the BlueStar install doc specs that they are saying this is not an issue with 6'' of ceramic tile over drywall vertically above and below the cooktop surface. Bottom line - the 6'' backguard is ugly and would cover a good amount of a backsplash design we currently have, and look ridiculous. title: Small Talk. | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "bbstxx", "author_name": "bbstx", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/bbstxx", "date": "2026-02-27", "text": "In a thread within the past few weeks (I can\u2019t remember what the topic was or who started the thread),  Mtn mentioned that someone once told her the point of small talk was that it was small talk.  Below is taken from yesterday\u2019s NYT Well newsletter.  I could\u2019t find a way to link the article, so I just copied it.  I thought it was interesting and maybe something to practice. The big benefits of small talk By Jancee Dunn A few months ago, my parents visited me at The New York Times. As we rode the elevator to my floor, my father greeted almost everyone who stepped inside. For my dad, strangers in an elevator are merely friends he hasn\u2019t met. To a guy toting a large cup of coffee: \u201cThat\u2019ll get your brain going!\u201d To a woman I recognized from the Styles section: \u201cYour sneakers are terrific!\u201d \u201cOh my god, Dad,\u201d I whispered, suddenly 16 again. I\u2019m not quite as chatty as he is, but I do understand why my father does this: It makes your world friendlier. Gillian Sandstrom, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Sussex and author of the upcoming book \u201cOnce Upon a Stranger: The Science of How \u2018Small Talk\u2019 Can Add Up to a Big Life,\u201d has been studying the effects of talking to strangers for the last 16 years. She has found that it can increase your well-being, improve your social skills, reduce anxiety and social biases and make you feel more connected. A self-described introvert and a formerly \u201cincredibly shy person,\u201d Dr. Sandstrom said that plucking up the courage to talk to people she doesn\u2019t know had changed her life. By talking to strangers, Dr. Sandstrom has met a volunteer who administers first aid to bats as well as a sperm-bank manager. These sorts of chance exchanges, she said, add novelty, different perspectives, unexpected recommendations and learning opportunities into our lives, making them more \u201cpsychologically rich.\u201d Here are Dr. Sandstrom\u2019s tips on how to chat up strangers. Pick people whose \u2018interests are visible\u2019 To minimize discomfort, choose a place that provides a limited time for both of you, she said \u2014 say, a train platform or a checkout line rather than the beginning of a trans-Atlantic flight. Choose a person who seems receptive. For instance, you might smile and see if it\u2019s returned, she said. An easy shortcut to conversation, Dr. Sandstrom said, is to look for someone who is displaying their interests: a band T-shirt, a museum tote bag, an antique brooch. Then simply ask about it, she said. When Dr. Sandstrom spots a person reading a book on the Tube in London, she will wait for the reader to put the book down and then ask if it\u2019s good. \u201cI\u2019ve found people love to give recommendations,\u201d she said. While she said there was no perfect way to start a conversation, a good formula was to ask a question, find something in common or extend a kindness such as an offer to help. Follow your curiosity If you\u2019re genuinely intrigued by something that someone is doing, it\u2019s usually \u201cworth the awkwardness\u201d of asking about it, Dr. Sandstrom said. \u201cIf someone is eating something delicious-looking at a restaurant, ask what it is,\u201d she writes in the book. \u201cIf you see a line snaking down the block, ask someone what they\u2019re waiting for.\u201d Usually, people will be happy to share what they\u2019re doing, she said. Pretend you\u2019re a regular If you\u2019re feeling a little nervous, one way to take the leap is to pretend you\u2019re a frequent customer in an unfamiliar place, Dr. Sandstrom said. In one of her studies, which took place in a coffee shop, she had one group hand money to the cashier with little interaction, while the other group was told to act like a regular \u2014 smile, make eye contact and have a genuine social interaction. The ones who acted like regulars were able to comfortably talk to strangers, and they felt greater happiness and a sense of belonging. This is how Hardi Plank outdoor siding is described: \"Its composition actually allows it to absorb some moisture and then dry back out without damage. However, there are caveats: Hardie is water-resistant, not completely waterproof. If water gets behind the siding (for example, if flashing or caulk fails) or if cut edges are left unsealed, moisture can eventually cause issues over years. In freezing climates, panels that stay wet at the bottom (splash zones) can gradually delaminate if not trimmed or protected. In practice, this risk is low if siding is installed with proper house wrap, trim, and caulking.\" I did see the results of a test that was started back in 2016 comparing Hardi Plank siding vs. a different type of siding (not vinyl).  A piece of each siding was cut and sealed in a thick plastic container - the bottom of each was left continuously in 2-3\" of water to see what happened. The non Hardi type of siding basically doubled in size - and wicked all the way up the sample.  The Hardi Plank siding had not changed - the part immersed in water was the same thickness as the top + measured the same thickness as the original product. Now - I am not suggesting that people use this in their showers/tub surrounds - however, it apparently will hold up as long as it was installed + maintained correctly.  The big issue is what has happened BEHIND the Hardi Plank. If the shower/tub surrounds were completely waterproofed (similarly as would be done prior to tile installation) - the interior walls/framing/etc. would be protected the same way as when tile is used.  After all, you can shower inside a properly waterproofed shower stall - BEFORE any tile/grout has been installed - without causing any issues/damage.  No one would leave it that way because it looks unattractive. I guess using Hardi Planks is sort of similar to the current trend to use micro-cement and Venetian plaster in showers (need a waterproof membrane behind the micro-cement). Below is a DIY micro-cement project by Jenna Sue Design:   While micro-cement itself is not waterproof, it is water-resistant. This means that water will bead and roll off the surface rather than soaking in, which is why it works well in spaces like bathrooms. Additionally, micro-cement is a breathable material. If moisture does manage to penetrate the surface, the material allows it to evaporate naturally, preventing long-term damage. This micro-cement breathability is similar to what you might experience with concrete, natural stone, or grout lines in tiles. OR- Venetian Plaster:   After the walls and floors are completely waterproofed, Venetian plaster may be applied straight to the shower walls.  The substrate prep directions are exactly the same as surface waterproof membranes that are used on shower walls prior to the installation of tile. There are also sealers that are used over lime plaster/Venetian plaster (some are waterproof - and some are water resistant and allow the plaster to breathe). Tadelakt showers: an ancient lime plaster finish. Color Atelier has a product called \"Tadelakt\" (tadelakt is a process used to do walls - but this company has made a special product that makes it easier to use inside showers).  There is a chemical reaction that occurs between the lime and olive oil soap that creates a hydrophobic seal (needs to be reapplied every couple years).", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b0f2257409a4bc37_3770-w240-h122-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/e242004c09a4bc38_3771-w240-h366-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/9d2211a509a4bc39_3770-w240-h362-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/616236a509a4bc3a_3771-w240-h239-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/b30219f809a4bc3b_3774-w240-h300-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: How To Choose A Builder To Know I’m Getting A Good Deal? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-621709943", "author_name": "Joe Saleen", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-621709943", "date": "2026-02-27", "text": "I\u2019ve talked to a number of builders in my area (Montgomery County, Texas) and found many that are impressive. Several of interest to me are design/build firms.  What I\u2019m having trouble with is the concept that they usually employ which is going in for an initial consultation and estimate, and then signing an agreement to spend 5 to $10,000 with them to develop detailed plans that they can come up with a fixed price number on. Unless I\u2019m willing to spend that kind of money with several builders and then compare final costs between them, how do I know that the one that I\u2019ve chosen to go forward with initially is giving me the best price?Another option that I\u2019ve considered is to hire an architect to develop plans and go out for bid to several contractors. I don\u2019t know if all design/ build firms are like this, but one specifically told me that they\u2019re not interested in working with me if I\u2019m going out for competitive bids.I\u2019m interested in perspectives from owners as well as builders.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "author_name": "Charles Ross Homes", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1291890641", "date": "2026-02-28", "text": "Hi, Joe, As owner of a residential design/build company, I appreciate your dilemma, albeit from the other side of the table, so to speak. First, design/build--whether performed on a fixed-contract price or cost-plus basis-- is best done as an \"open book\" process with full visibility of costs including the builder's overhead and profit.   Ask each company you're considering what their overhead and profit is when building on a fixed-contract price basis.  If they build on a cost-plus basis ask what the \"plus\" is. After covid-19, we changed from building on a fixed-contract price to a fixed-management fee basis.  Our clients pay for all of the costs associated with building their home plus our fixed fee to management the process.  While they're at risk for increases in material or subcontracted labor versus our estimate, we don't put any more in our pocket when those occur. Estimating construction costs is a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem:  the builder can't produce a reasonably accurate estimate without plans, and the client doesn't want to spend money to produce plans for a home that won't get built.   We do cost benchmarking prior to design.  Our benchmarking process compares plans and actual construction costs for homes we've built in the last year or two which are similar to what the client has in mind.  For each plan, we determine what is different from the client's intended home design and make estimates of the cost of those differences (e.g., three-car vs. two-car garage, larger home footprint, site work costs, etc.)  Then we add an amount for whatever construction cost inflation we've had in our market since the homes were built.  It's not perfect, but it's a fairly quick reality check before investing anything in a design.", "images": []}}
